questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a two-case comparison controlled
questions.learningObjective: Identify what controls a two-case comparison
questions.stem: An analyst compares two factories with identical machinery but different shift lengths.

options.text: The comparison is controlled because machinery is held constant while shift length varies.
The comparison is controlled because the factories are in the same industry.
The comparison is controlled because both factories produce the same product.
options.misconception: confuses product with the controlled factor

options.text: The comparison is uncontrolled because two factories can never be compared.

questions.explanation: A controlled comparison holds key factors constant while varying one. Matching machinery isolates shift length as the difference.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Distinguishing a controlled pair from a juxtaposition
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish controlled comparison from juxtaposition
questions.stem: An analyst places two dashboard notes side by side without matching any variables.

answer.exemplar: Placing two cases side by side without matching variables is a juxtaposition, not a controlled comparison; it can suggest patterns but cannot support causal claims because confounders remain unaddressed.

questions.explanation: Juxtaposition presents cases without control. It may spark ideas but cannot isolate causes.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A variable measured the same way in two cases
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the need for identical measurement

stimulus.body: The dashboard note shows two regions with response times recorded in minutes for one and seconds for the other. The analyst labels both as fast.

questions.stem: Two cases report speed in different units, yet the analyst calls both fast.

options.text: The comparison is valid because the analyst used the same word for both.
The comparison works if the analyst converts mentally.
The comparison fails because the units differ and cannot be compared directly.
The comparison is fine because both values are small numbers.

questions.explanation: A variable must be measured the same way in both cases. Different units make the comparison meaningless without conversion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR

questions.stem: Two similar clinics show different recovery rates, and one serves a poorer neighbourhood.

options.text: The difference in recovery is due to clinic quality alone.
The difference is random and needs no explanation.
The clinics cannot be compared because they are in different places.
The neighbourhood's resources may explain the diverging outcome.

questions.explanation: A contextual difference like neighbourhood resources can drive diverging outcomes even when clinics look similar. It must be examined before attributing cause.
questions.hint: Check the context behind the divergence.

options.text: The third site tests whether the mechanism holds when the condition changes.
Testing a third site is unnecessary because two cases already agree.
The third site should match the first two exactly to be useful.
The mechanism is proven once it is stated clearly.

questions.explanation: Testing the mechanism where the condition changes checks whether it is general or limited. Replication alone cannot do that.

questions.explanation: A contextual difference like client mix can drive diverging churn even when dashboards look similar. It must be examined first.
